whatItFakes: A counted member's marital status and which relative is their child: a woman is married when an adult relative within the minimum parent age of her age lives in her household, and a mother when a relative under 5 is at least that much younger.
why: The counts keep family pairs without their kind and carry no marital status, so the web's mothers and married-women outcomes cannot read a counted woman's own record.
replacement: Counted members' partner and parent-child links kept in the counts, read in place of the age rule.

whatItFakes: Local immigration enforcement (enforcement-to-undocumented-employment, enforcement-to-us-born-employment) reaches workers through the jobs engine's pull to work, by a work authorization seeded on who each noncitizen is (isUnauthorized in src/core2/citizenship.ts), at one national share of noncitizens who are unauthorized (parameter unauthorizedShareOfNoncitizens, Pew 2024) rather than each state's. Citizens stand for the U.S.-born the research measures, since the core records no birthplace, so naturalized citizens take the U.S.-born effect. Only the pull to work reads it; no employer checks authorization at hire.
why: Pew publishes the unauthorized population by state but no table here holds each state's noncitizens to divide it by, and people are generated without a birthplace.
replacement: A per-state unauthorized share of noncitizens (Pew state estimates over ACS noncitizens, table B05001) in place data, and a seeded nativity on people (full and counted) so naturalized citizens are told from the U.S.-born.

whatItFakes: The minimum-wage-to-low-wage-jobs link needs the minimum wage as a share of the place's median wage (labor.minimum-wage-to-median), which no engine records.
why: The wage floor is read by the jobs engine for pay, but the ratio to the median is not a kept measure.
replacement: A reader in the jobs engine of the wage floor over the place's median hourly pay, added to the engine measures.
resolution: gov-measures.ts records labor.minimum-wage-to-median (the governing minimum wage over the median hourly pay of the town's current jobs), and the web's model counts government measures as causes (src/core2/gov-measure-keys.ts), so minimum-wage-to-low-wage-jobs runs. Its reach to employers is SG-LABOR-low-wage-unreviewed's.

whatItFakes: Birth-year pollution (birth-year-pollution-to-adult-earnings), teacher quality (teacher-quality-to-earnings) and neighborhood years (neighborhood-years-to-adult-outcomes) acting on adult earnings move nothing, each for its own missing piece. Birth-year pollution: the exposure is on record for anyone born in play (a person:birth fact with place and date, src/core2/births-people.ts, and the web's month rows of env.particulates for that place), but no pay decision reads it and the link has no size. Teacher quality: nothing records a teacher's value-added or which teacher a student has, and no law or engine moves teacher value-added, so the cause has no producer and no policy to carry. Neighborhood years: where each person lived each year is on record (residenceOn in src/core2/past-moves.ts, and moves in play), but no data row holds a county's childhood exposure effect, no pay decision reads it and the link has no size.
why: The links are person-level (exposure-years shape): a place rate would apply them to the wrong people, so each must be read from the person's own history when pay is set.
replacement: Birth-year pollution: a read in src/core2/jobs-web.ts of the person's birth fact and the web's particulates over their birth year, sized from its study. Teacher quality: parked until a researched link moves teacher value-added (a teacher-pay or evaluation law); then the school engine keeps a value-added per teacher and a yearly classroom, and hirePay reads its mean. Neighborhood years: a county row of childhood exposure effects, read in hirePay from residenceOn and in-play moves.

whatItFakes: Transit loss to unemployment (transit-loss-to-unemployment), broadband to employment (broadband-to-employment), incentive deals to industry jobs (incentive-deal-to-industry-jobs) and more immigrants to the workforce (more-immigration-to-workforce) have no researched size the game can use, and a Medicaid work requirement's effect on employment (work-requirement-to-employment) is about zero, so an engine would multiply by one.
why: Their sources give a study-unit effect (one lost line, a county gaining broadband, one deal) that no conversion turns into the game's slopes; the sizes are to confirm.
replacement: Sizes confirmed from the sources and the cause measures (transit access, deal records) recorded by their engines.

whatItFakes: Pretrial detention lowering the pull to formal work (pretrial-detention-to-employment): the jobs engine adds the log of one plus the row's size to the choice score of anyone the justice engine first held while they waited for a hearing, from the row's lag on and for good. The research measures the gap three to four years after the hearing, not how long it lasts or whether a second detention adds to it, and every job the jobs engine keeps stands for formal employment because it keeps no informal work. A counted member carries no term: the justice engine files counted defendants as cases by group (CountedCaseRow, detained as a count), and the counts keep no record of which member was held.
why: Dobbie, Goldin and Yang (2018) compare formal employment three to four years after the bail hearing; the game has no informal work to set it against, and the counted tier's detention is a head count per case, not a record of a member the jobs engine could read.
replacement: A duration from the research on the term; a record of which counted member was held, for the counted tier to read as a named person's is; and the term fitted in a played year so detained defendants' share at work runs the researched 20% under that of those released (see SG-LABOR-participation-scale).

whatItFakes: The size of the web's participation effects on mothers and married women at work, and of the pull to formal work of anyone the justice engine first held while they waited for a hearing (pretrial-detention-to-employment): the engine adds the log of the factor to a deterministic choice score, which reaches the records but is not fitted to the researched size. The older workers' term has its own fitted weight (jobsOlderWorkWebWeight).
why: Measured in a played town: an older-work effect of +0.3 (a 30% change in the researched outcome) moved the share of 62 to 67 year olds at work from 0.656 to 0.677, about 3%, because the choice scores are logistic and the entry and exit pulls are small.
replacement: A weight on the term, fitted in a played year so each group's share moves by the researched size (mothers, married women), as jobsOlderWorkWebWeight is for ages 62 to 66.

whatItFakes: defense-contracts-to-earnings does nothing: its cause federal.defense-boost-pct (extra defense contracts as a share of the state's output) is not recorded by any engine, so the link never runs; the pay level already reads labor.median-earnings and will carry it once the cause exists.
why: No federal procurement engine records state contract awards.
replacement: A federal spending engine recording each state's defense contract awards, read as federal.defense-boost-pct.
resolution: The budgets module records the federal national defense line, and defenseBoostPct (src/core2/gov-measures.ts) reads it above its base, as a share, times the state's fiscal 2024 defense contracts per resident over its output per resident (data/research/federal/defense-contracts-by-state-fy2024.json), read by the web as federal.defense-boost-pct (reader defense-boost-pct, src/core2/modules/outcome-web.ts). The link runs, and the jobs engine's pay level (payLevel in src/core2/modules/jobs.ts) multiplies by its labor.median-earnings factor when it prices an opening and when it raises a worker, shown in law-wiring-labor-web.test.ts.

whatItFakes: minimum-wage-to-low-wage-jobs and federal-minimum-wage-to-low-wage-jobs scale only the staffing targets of employers the jobs engine reviews, and in played towns none of those has a job under the line; the town's low-wage jobs belong to organizations the review never reaches, so the factor moves no record.
why: In a bench world (Sail Harbor, Connecticut, seed 6bad944e1a974146) all 32 reviewed employers had no heads under the line while about 190 of the town's 208 low-wage jobs sat with organizations outside the employers table; summed staffing need was identical to 15 digits with the factor at 0.5.
replacement: The jobs engine applies the low-wage factor to every organization whose jobs labor.low-wage-jobs counts, at the moment it sets that organization's staffing, shown in a low-wage-only twin by employer id.
